source_title: Policy on Compassionate Leave for Postgraduate Research Degree students

primary.question: One of our PGR students has been bereaved. What leave can they take, and what happens if they need longer than that?
primary.expected_answer: Compassionate leave can be sought for up to two weeks (10 working days), and the standard and maximum periods of study and the thesis submission date are automatically extended by the duration of the approved compassionate leave. If the longer-term impact requires a longer period of leave, the Policy on Leave of Absence (intermission) should be consulted instead - that is a separate policy with its own grounds and procedures.
primary.actual_answer:
For a bereaved PGR student, there are two options depending on how much time they need:

**Short-term: Compassionate Leave**
- Covers bereavement or serious illness/injury of a close relative, dependant, or friend, for the immediate/short-term impact.
- Can be granted for up to two weeks (10 working days).
- The student (or their supervisor, if the student can't make the request themselves) should apply by emailing the PGRE Team (pgresearch@essex.ac.uk), ideally after first contacting their supervisor for support and advice.
- The student's standard and maximum period of study, and their thesis submission date, are automatically extended by the length of approved compassionate leave.
- This is distinct from intermission or sickness absence, and separate from any studentship funding terms or the Special Leave Policy (for students who are also staff).

**If longer leave is needed: Leave of Absence (Intermission)**
- If the longer-term impact of the bereavement requires more time than two weeks, the student should instead apply under the Policy on Leave of Absence (Intermission) for PGR students, covering "domestic/family problems relating to serious ill-health, death, and/or the need to provide care."
- A term's leave is usually granted initially, with the situation reassessed towards the end of that period.
- A maximum of 3 terms of non-medical intermission can be granted in total; beyond that, the student would be required to withdraw and could apply for readmission later.
- If the minimum period of study hasn't been completed, and the course permits, the student may have the option to switch from full-time to part-time status instead (though visa requirements may prevent this for overseas students).

Sources:
- https://www.essex.ac.uk/-/media/documents/about/governance/policy-on-compassional-leave-for-research-degree-students.pdf
- https://www.essex.ac.uk/-/media/documents/directories/academic-section/pgre/pgr-intermission-absence.pdf

primary.question: A PGR student sponsored on a Student visa wants to intermit for two terms. What are the consequences?
primary.expected_answer: The University is required to withdraw sponsorship from a student who intermits, and the Home Office will curtail their immigration permission. The student will have to leave the UK while intermitting, and must stop any work immediately because the condition allowing work alongside study no longer applies. Before returning they can request further immigration sponsorship and, if eligible, apply for a new Student visa. Retrospective intermission is not possible for sponsored students.
primary.actual_answer:
For a PGR student sponsored on a Student visa, intermitting for two terms would trigger these consequences:

- **Loss of visa sponsorship**: The University is required to withdraw sponsorship from a student who intermits, and the Home Office will curtail (cut short) their immigration permission.
- **Must leave the UK**: The student will have to leave the UK for the duration of the intermission, since they cannot be in the UK while not fully registered and actively engaged in study.
- **Must stop working**: If they have been working, they must stop immediately, as the condition permitting work alongside study no longer applies once sponsorship is withdrawn.
- **Re-sponsorship needed to return**: Prior to returning to studies in the UK, the student can request further immigration sponsorship and, if eligible, apply for a new Student visa to re-enter the UK.
- **Home Office reporting**: A report will be made to the Home Office when this happens, and the International Services Team will notify the student by email and provide immigration advice.
- **No retrospective intermission**: Sponsored students cannot be granted retrospective intermission, due to Home Office timescales for reporting changes, the requirement not to be in/have been in the UK while not fully registered, and Home Office engagement-monitoring guidance.

Note: if a short absence can be agreed without formal intermission or an extension to course duration, it may be possible for the student to remain sponsored during that period instead — but this is different from a two-term intermission, which would trigger the consequences above.

Source: https://www.essex.ac.uk/-/media/documents/directories/academic-section/pgre/pgr-intermission-absence.pdf

primary.question: Our student intends to submit their thesis at the end of their completion period. What do they need to do in advance, and how much notice is required?
primary.expected_answer: They must give the Postgraduate Research Education Team at least three months' notice of their intention to submit, via the Approval of Title form, which the PGRE Team needs to begin appointing examiners. Submitting it late is likely to delay the examination process. A student entering a completion period does so on the understanding that the full thesis will be ready for submission by the end of that period.
primary.actual_answer:
Before submitting, the student must give the Postgraduate Research Education Team at least **three months' notice** of their intention to submit, using the **Approval of Title form**. This form triggers the process of appointing examiners — if it isn't submitted at least three months before submission, delays to the appointment of examiners (and thus the examination process) are likely.

Additionally, all registration fees and debts must be paid before the thesis can be accepted for submission, and the thesis must be submitted electronically in PDF format (as a single document, emailed to pgrsubmission@essex.ac.uk).

On timing of the deadline itself: for candidates first registered from October 2018 onwards, the standard submission deadline is the end of the standard period of study, but if a completion period has been recommended by the Supervisory Panel and Research Students' Progress Board and approved by the Faculty Dean, the deadline shifts — for a one or two-term completion period, the new deadline is the end of that approved completion period; if a third term of completion is approved, the deadline is four weeks prior to the end of that third term.

This reduction will not apply if exceptional circumstances make it inappropriate to reduce completion periods in that way.

In both cases, students must be offered an opportunity to discuss this with the RSPB before the final recommendation is forwarded to the Dean for approval.

primary.question: A first-year PGR student is asking for three terms of leave. Is that possible, and is there a shorter option?
primary.expected_answer: It is possible but consequential: if a student requests a leave of absence during their first year of study which extends for longer than two terms, they will be required to restart the course. For short-term needs following bereavement or the serious illness of a close relative, compassionate leave of up to two weeks is a separate and lighter-touch option that automatically extends the study periods and submission date.
primary.actual_answer:
For a first-year PGR student, requesting three terms of leave would trigger a specific restriction: **if a leave of absence during the first year of study extends for longer than two terms, the student will be required to restart the course.** So three terms of intermission in the first year is possible in principle (it doesn't exceed the general maximum of 3 terms of non-medical intermission, or 9 terms for medical intermission), but the consequence is that the student would have to restart the course rather than simply resume where they left off.

As for a shorter option: **compassionate leave** is available for up to two weeks (10 working days) and is distinct from intermission - it's a quicker, less disruptive route for short-term needs (e.g., bereavement or a personal crisis), applied for by emailing the PGRE Team (pgresearch@essex.ac.uk). It doesn't carry the "restart the course" consequence that a longer intermission in year one would. If the underlying issue is likely to need more than two weeks but the student wants to avoid restarting, they should discuss with their supervisor whether a leave of two terms or less might suffice, since anything beyond two terms in the first year forces a restart.

primary.question: A thesis was referred and the student has now resubmitted. Do we need an Independent Chair for the second viva, and can the viva be waived?
primary.expected_answer: Two separate rules apply. An Independent Chair is appointed where the viva follows a referral and resubmission of a thesis, so yes. On waiving, where the recommendation on the referred thesis is a pass, a request by the examiners to waive the viva will normally be granted; where the recommendation is not a pass, a waiver will only be granted in exceptional circumstances.
primary.actual_answer:
**Independent Chair:** Yes — under the Policy for the Appointment of Independent Chairs for Research Degree Vivas, the Faculty Dean Postgraduate will appoint an Independent Chair when "the viva is following a referral and resubmission of a thesis" (https://www.essex.ac.uk/-/media/documents/about/governance/independent-chairs-policy.pdf).

**Waiving the viva:** It's possible but harder than for a first submission. Per the Code of Practice for Postgraduate Research, for a referred thesis:
- If the examiners' recommended outcome is a **pass**, a request to waive the viva will **normally be granted**.
- If the recommendation is **not a pass**, waiving the viva will **only be granted in exceptional circumstances**.

In either case, if a waiver is approved, the Postgraduate Research Education Team must notify the student of the examiners' request and reasons, and the student must be told they still have the right to insist on a viva if they wish (https://www.essex.ac.uk/-/media/documents/about/governance/code-practice-postgraduate-research.pdf).

primary.question: We want a visiting academic to supervise a research student. Could they instead act as Independent Chair at a viva?
primary.expected_answer: Visiting staff cannot be appointed as a supervisor of a PGR student unless formally appointed via the associate supervisor route. Nor could they be an Independent Chair: a nominee must be a permanent member of staff who has been an Internal Examiner for at least two postgraduate research examinations at Essex, or has examined two theses externally and undertaken University of Essex Independent Chair training.
primary.actual_answer:
The policies I can see don't directly address whether a visiting academic could act as Independent Chair, but the eligibility criteria and appointment rules make this very unlikely to be possible.

The Independent Chairs Policy specifies that a candidate for the pool must:
- **be a permanent member of staff** who has been an Internal Examiner for at least two postgraduate research examinations at Essex; or has examined two theses externally and undertaken University of Essex Independent Chair training (when available); and
- have a good understanding of the University's procedures and regulations for the award being examined.

A visiting academic would not typically be a "permanent member of staff," which is an explicit requirement, so on that basis they would not qualify.

Separately, even if this hurdle were overcome, there is a conflict-of-interest rule: "the Independent Chair chosen will be from outside the candidate's department and will have no conflict of interest with the candidate, the supervisor or the External Examiner." Since you're asking about this person specifically because they would be supervising the student, they would have a direct conflict of interest as the supervisor and could not act as Independent Chair for that same candidate's viva regardless of their staffing status.

So the same visiting academic could not both supervise a student and serve as Independent Chair at that student's viva.

follow_up.question: Can the supervisor sit in to support the inexperienced examiner?
follow_up.expected_answer: Not normally. The candidate's supervisor will not normally be present at the viva and can only be present in exceptional circumstances, approved on an individual basis by the Faculty Dean (Postgraduate) and with the agreement of the examiners. It is good practice for the supervisor to be invited in at the end when the examiners communicate their recommendation.
follow_up.actual_answer:
No. The supervisor's attendance at the viva is governed entirely by the candidate's circumstances, not by whether the examiner is experienced — an inexperienced internal examiner is instead addressed by the Faculty Dean (Postgraduate) appointing an **Independent Chair** to oversee proceedings, not by having the supervisor sit in.

The supervisor "will not normally be present" at the viva, and can only attend in exceptional circumstances, approved individually by the Faculty Dean (Postgraduate) and with the agreement of the examiner(s) and the candidate. The normal practice is instead that the supervisor is encouraged to be nearby in the department to support the candidate afterward, and may be invited in at the very end, with permission, when the result is communicated.

So there is no provision for the supervisor to sit in specifically to support or assist an inexperienced examiner — that gap is filled by the Independent Chair role instead.

source_title: Policy on Thesis Submission, Deposit and Retention

primary.question: How should a professional doctorate candidate submit their thesis, and what happens next in the examination process?
primary.expected_answer: All candidates for Masters by Dissertation, MPhil, MD, PhD and Professional Doctorate must submit the thesis electronically in PDF format, contained within one document rather than separate files, emailed to the Postgraduate Research Team at pgrsubmission@essex.ac.uk, with all registration fees and debts paid first. The examination then proceeds to the viva, whose format is agreed between the participants starting from the candidate's preference.
primary.actual_answer:
Based on the thesis submission and deposit rules and the Code of Practice for Professional Doctorates:

**Submission process:**
- The candidate first needs an approved title. The supervisor and Head of Department approve the proposed title, and the Approval of Title form must be submitted to the Postgraduate Research Education Team at least three months prior to submission, to allow time to appoint examiners — late submission of the title risks delaying the appointment of examiners and the examination process.
- Following title approval, the candidate is sent an RD1: Submission form for the thesis.
- The thesis must be submitted electronically in PDF format, contained within a single document (not split into separate PDF files), and emailed as specified in the guidance.

**What happens next:**
- Examiners are nominated/appointed per the Guidelines for the Appointment of Research Examiners.
- Before the viva, the internal and external examiners each independently complete an Initial Report Form with their preliminary assessment of the thesis, submitted to the Postgraduate Research Education Team at least one week before the viva, who then arrange for the reports to be exchanged.
- A viva voce examination takes place, giving the candidate the chance to defend the thesis; the candidate typically leaves the room while examiners confer on the outcome and is then told the result. If a face-to-face viva isn't possible, the Dean's permission is needed to hold it via video link. In certain circumstances (e.g., examination by external examiners only, or following an appeal) the Dean may appoint an Independent Chair to attend, though this person is not an examiner of the thesis.
- After the viva, examiners complete a Joint Report Form recording the outcome. If corrections are required, examiners provide a list of corrections with the Joint Report to the Postgraduate Research Education Team for approval by the Dean.
- Candidates can request copies of the examiners' pre- and post-viva reports once examining is complete.
- The Dean then seeks confirmation from the PD Director that all components of the professional doctorate programme have been completed.
- If a candidate disagrees with the examination outcome, they may appeal via the Appeals Procedures for Postgraduate Research Students.

Sources:
- https://www.essex.ac.uk/-/media/documents/about/governance/code-practice-professional-doctorates.pdf
- https://www.essex.ac.uk/-/media/documents/about/governance/thesis-submission-deposit.pdf
